prize_parts.citation: for establishing liquid-liquid phase separation as a physical-chemical principle that organizes the interior of living cells
for the design of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enable delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Both parts rest on concepts of molecular organisation that physical chemistry made quantitative. Hyman and Brangwynne showed with the P-granule work that cellular compartments can be liquid phases governed by multivalent interactions and phase behaviour, a concept that has been reproduced in very many systems and that links to amyloid-type transitions and disease. Cullis and the Vancouver lipid work turned pKa-dependent charge, lipid self-assembly and membrane fusion into a delivery technology that is validated at global scale (siRNA drugs, mRNA vaccines). Together they would honour how soft-matter and colloid chemistry underpins both cell biology and medicine, areas where physical chemistry is under-represented relative to synthesis.
statement.case_against: Phase separation is the least settled of my choices on maturity: the physiological relevance of many reported condensates is contested and some in vitro or in vivo assays have proved artefact-prone, and it may be judged biology rather than chemistry. The lipid nanoparticle part has diffuse and patent-entangled credit across Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and naming Cullis alone excludes people with real claims. In a combined prize I also drop Rosen, Pappu and Mittag, whose multivalency and sequence-grammar work gives the physical-chemistry foundation, which is a genuine cost to the first part.

responses.point: Ranked phase separation fourth and flagged that its physiological relevance is actively debated and that timing may be slightly early.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it is why I now narrow the credit to Hyman and Brangwynne, whose demonstration of liquid-like P granules is the best-reproduced core, and do not rest the case on every condensate claim. Where I disagree is that the debate is about which condensates matter functionally, not about whether liquid-liquid demixing is a real organising principle; the concept is secure even if particular examples fail. I would like to hear which specific claims you consider artefactual before accepting 'too early'.

responses.point: Ranked targeted protein degradation first as a general molecular-design principle with clinical consequences, and ranked ionizable lipid nanoparticles second, noting that credit there is spread and patent-entangled.
responses.response: I agree on lipid nanoparticles and their chemistry, and on the attribution problem, which I think is solved best by anchoring on the Vancouver ionizable-lipid formulation work rather than splitting credit across the whole field. On degraders I agree the principle is strong, but with no approved PROTAC and the credit split between the PROTAC and molecular-glue branches (Crews, Deshaies, Handa, Ciulli, Gray), I see it as less ripe than the nanoparticle case, so I keep it as an alternative rather than my lead. If the committee wants a medicinal-chemistry prize, I would not oppose B066.

responses.point: Ranked Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first, as a general, overdue method with clean two-person attribution (Buchwald and Hartwig), distinct from the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
responses.response: The attribution is indeed the cleanest on the shortlist and the maturity argument is unanswerable. My reservation is conceptual overlap: the 2010 prize already recognised Pd cross-coupling as a strategy, and a second prize on the same catalyst family might leave soft matter and biophysical themes unrepresented for another decade. I do not think this is disqualifying and would support B038 if the committee wants a clean, mature synthetic prize, which is why it is my second alternative.

responses.point: Ranked halide perovskite solar cell absorbers first for a new materials capability with a clear physical basis, while noting disputed 2012 attribution and unresolved stability and lead toxicity.
responses.response: I agree the science is striking and the physical basis is clear, but the six-name attribution problem you describe, with near-simultaneous 2012 contributions, makes any trio contestable, and long-term stability is not resolved. I would prefer a discovery whose attribution we can defend; I am not persuaded that efficiency growth alone makes it the strongest chemistry candidate, but I would like to see how others weigh the Miyasaka versus Park and Seok question.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept phase separation as chemistry rather than cell biology or physiology.
Whether the 2023 Medicine prize on mRNA modification weakens the case for a delivery-chemistry prize.
Whether a single name (Cullis) is defensible for lipid nanoparticles given Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer.
Whether Rosen should replace Brangwynne or be added in a single-part prize on B036 alone.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. I sit on the committee with Lund colleagues Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and lipid self-assembly is my own research field, so I am professionally close to the lipid nanoparticle and phase-separation literature, but I have no personal or institutional tie to the named candidates that requires recusal.
